why: Kahn's algorithm produces the order itself, not just a yes/no: repeatedly output a course whose prerequisites are all done. Using a min-heap for the ready set makes the order the lexicographically smallest one, and an order shorter than numCourses means a cycle.
hints: Which courses can you take on day one? After taking one, which new courses become possible?
Count each course's unfinished prerequisites (its in-degree). A course is ready at 0. Taking it decrements every course that depends on it.

Push all in-degree-0 courses into a min-heap; pop the smallest, append it, decrement its successors, push those that reach 0. If the result has fewer than numCourses entries, return []. O((V + E) log V).
pitfalls: The pair is [course, prerequisite]: the edge goes prerequisite -> course.
A plain queue gives a valid order but not the smallest one; the tie rule needs a heap.
